source_refs.note: Book p. 270: 14.2.4 properties (i)-(v) of the dot product. Book error: (i) printed as u.v = 0 => u = 0 or v = 0 (false; u perpendicular to v also gives 0). Reasons, checks, tips, mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: Let \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) be vectors and let \(c\) be any real number, then

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
Property (i) as printed, "\(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0 \Rightarrow \underline{u} = \underline{0}\) or \(\underline{v} = \underline{0}\)", is false for vectors. For example \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{j} = 0\) although neither \(\underline{i}\) nor \(\underline{j}\) is the zero vector. The correct statement is:
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0 \iff \underline{u} = \underline{0} \text{ or } \underline{v} = \underline{0}\]
\[\text{or } \underline{u} \perp \underline{v}\]
For non-zero vectors, \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\) means exactly that \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are perpendicular (14.2.6).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why each property holds (write \(\underline{u} = a_{1}\underline{i} + b_{1}\underline{j} + c_{1}\underline{k}\), and similarly for \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\); the component formula is in 14.2.5):
(ii) \(a_{1}a_{2} + b_{1}b_{2} + c_{1}c_{2} = a_{2}a_{1} + b_{2}b_{1} + c_{2}c_{1}\), because numbers commute (also shown in 14.2.2 (c)).
(iii) Each component of \(\underline{v} + \underline{w}\) is a sum, e.g. \(a_{2} + a_{3}\); then \(a_{1}(a_{2} + a_{3}) = a_{1}a_{2} + a_{1}a_{3}\), and the same for the other components.
(iv) \(c\underline{u}\) has components \(ca_{1}, cb_{1}, cc_{1}\), so every term has the common factor \(c\).
(v) The angle between \(\underline{u}\) and itself is \(0\): \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{u} = |\underline{u}||\underline{u}|\cos 0 = |\underline{u}|^{2}\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
A check of (iii) with numbers (ours): \(\underline{u} = \underline{i} + 2\underline{j}\), \(\underline{v} = 3\underline{i} - \underline{k}\), \(\underline{w} = \underline{j} + \underline{k}\).
\[\underline{v} + \underline{w} = 3\underline{i} + \underline{j} + 0\underline{k}\]
\[\underline{u} \cdot (\underline{v} + \underline{w}) = 3 + 2 + 0 = 5\]
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} + \underline{u} \cdot \underline{w} = 3 + 2 = 5\]
Both sides give \(5\).
Property (v) is the quickest way to find a magnitude: \(|\underline{u}| = \sqrt{\underline{u} \cdot \underline{u}}\); here \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{u} = 1 + 4 = 5\), so \(|\underline{u}| = \sqrt{5}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Commutative: \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = \underline{v} \cdot \underline{u}\).
2. Distributive: \(\underline{u} \cdot (\underline{v} + \underline{w}) = \underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} + \underline{u} \cdot \underline{w}\), so brackets open as in algebra.
3. Scalars come out: \((c\underline{u}) \cdot \underline{v} = c(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v})\).
4. \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{u} = |\underline{u}|^{2}\).
5. \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\) does not force a zero vector; it can mean \(\underline{u} \perp \underline{v}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Concluding from \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\) that one vector must be zero (the way \(ab = 0\) works for numbers). For vectors it may just mean that they are perpendicular.
2. "Cancelling" a vector: from \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = \underline{u} \cdot \underline{w}\) we cannot conclude \(\underline{v} = \underline{w}\); only that \(\underline{u} \perp (\underline{v} - \underline{w})\) (or \(\underline{u} = \underline{0}\)).
3. Writing \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{u} = |\underline{u}|\): it is \(|\underline{u}|^{2}\).
